newsitem.title: USA: Trial of reputed Mexican kingpin set to open.
newsitem.headline: Trial of reputed Mexican kingpin set to open.

text.p: The alleged head of Mexico's most notorious drug-smuggling cartel was set to go to trial in Houston on Monday on federal drug-trafficking, bribery and money-laundering charges.

Reputed drug kingpin Juan Garcia Abrego faced life in prison if convicted of smuggling billions of dollars worth of cocaine and marijuana across the U.S. border over the past 15 years for Colombia's Cali cartel.

Courthouse sources said there have been no signs of a plea bargain with Abrego, 51, who hinted to FBI agents after his arrest in January that he could name traffickers in Mexico's Gulf cartel responsible for massive cocaine shipments across the U.S. border.
"There has been no rumblings about a plea bargain," one source close to the case told Reuters. "I have seen no indication of that."

Abrego, one of the FBI's 10 most wanted criminals at the time of his capture, pleaded not guilty to the drug charges. His trial, which was to open in a federal courtroom on Monday with jury selection, was expected to last 10 weeks.

The Gulf cartel, which acted as a middle man for drugs from Colombia being shipped into the United States, emerged as one of the world's largest drug-smuggling operations during the administration of Mexican President Carlos Salinas. At the time Abrego was said to have made $50 million a month in political payoffs to avoid prosecution.

Abrego, known by the nickname El Senor -- "The Man" -- also was allegedly linked to the 1994 murder of a senior Mexican politician allegedly ordered by Raul Salinas de Gortari, who was awaiting trial in a Mexican jail.

In court filings U.S. prosecutors seemed more interested in seizing alleged drug proceeds from the reputed kingpin than negotiating a plea bargain for information on Mexican government corruption or operations of the Cali cartel.

Abrego was said to have amassed a $15 billion personal fortune from the tons of marijuana and cocaine smuggled by his Gulf cartel. In a 28-count indictment filed against Abrego and seven alleged cartel lieutenants, prosecutors sought forfeiture of at least $275 million in cash and property.

Mexican police in July seized four estates, 28 houses, two warehouses and 89 businesses believed owned by Abrego, who was captured on Jan. 14 by a camoflaged squad of drug agents on his ranch near the northern Mexico city of Monterrey.
Despite the prospect of a life sentence and the forfeiture of his personal fortune, Abrego through his attorneys said he will not cooperate with U.S. prosecutors.

Prosecutors planed to build their case on 51 months of wiretapped telephone conversations, stacks of shipping ledgers and business records and the testimony of convicted drug traffickers willing to trade evidence against Abrego for reduced sentences, according to court filings.

Assistant U.S. Attorney Melissa Annis, the chief prosecutor in the case, also was expected to introduce bank records detailing $30 million laundered through Swiss and Grand Cayman banks for the Gulf cartel.

The bank records first surfaced in an earlier trial of American Express Bank International banker Antonio Giraldi, Abrego's private banker who was convicted of money laundering in 1994 by a Texas jury.
